papers.title: Learning Fast Monomial Orders for Gröbner Basis Computations
papers.authors: R. Caleb Bunch, Alperen A. Ergür, Melika Golestani, Jessie Tong, Malia Walewski, Yunus E. Zeytuncu
papers.summary: Casts the choice of monomial order as a reinforcement-learning problem with actor/critic feed-forward networks; reward is actual F4 cost (Groebner.jl trace statistics incl. elimination-matrix column counts) estimated by Monte Carlo. Learned orders beat GrevLex on systems-biology and computer-vision benchmarks; no finite-field or cryptographic systems reported.
papers.relevance: Closest existing template for a learned presentation choice on lever 1: the Weil-descended S_{m+1} restricted to an l-dim subspace has a free choice of variable order / F_2-basis of V and of monomial order; the programme has shown d_F depends on presentation (PKM towers). An RL order-picker with msolve cost as reward is directly transplantable. Caveat: it changes constants and the measured D of a run, never the ideal; useful as an enabler for the unmeasured cells (4,4),(4,5),(4,6), not as an exponent lever.
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-1: on the (n,l,m)=(17..23, 3..5, 3) grid already measured, enumerate GL(l,F_2) basis changes of V and random variable permutations, record msolve degree profile and time; test whether any presentation lowers the certified last-fall degree (it should not: d_F is presentation-dependent only for PKM towers per the brief) and how far the time varies (log-variance = headroom for a learned picker). Falsifier: if headroom < 2x, drop.

papers.title: Letting Homogeneity Entropy Select S-Pairs in Buchberger's Algorithm
papers.authors: Uzma Shafiq, Matthew England, AmirHosein Sadeghimanesh, Nayyar Zaidi
papers.summary: Proposes an information-theoretic S-pair selection score (entropy of the degree distribution over an S-polynomial's monomials). Beats Degree/Normal/Sugar on random systems but loses on the PHCpack benchmark; authors conclude the right strategy is distribution-dependent.
papers.relevance: Shows hand-designed non-degree pair selection is live again; for F4 on descended Semaev systems (bihomogeneous, highly structured, S_m-symmetric) a selection tuned to the specific distribution could cut the dense intermediate degree. Engineering-level only.
papers.suggested_route: Fold into E-ML-1 as a baseline feature (entropy of degree spectrum of each pair) when logging msolve/F4 traces.

papers.title: HATSolver: Learning Groebner Bases with Hierarchical Attention Transformers
papers.authors: Mohamed Malhou, Ludovic Perret, Kristin Lauter
papers.summary: Extends Kera et al. (NeurIPS 2024) end-to-end transformer Gröbner-basis prediction with a tree-structured hierarchical attention and curriculum learning, solving larger instances than Kera et al.; cost analysis of the architecture. No accuracy figures or finite-field cryptographic systems in the abstract.
papers.relevance: Lauter/Perret entering Gröbner learning signals an intended cryptanalytic application (MQ/HFE-type). For ECDLP the systems are zero-dimensional with tiny solution sets; direct basis prediction is a lookup of the answer and cannot beat the generic oracle bound unless it uses field representation. Classify as engineering at best.
papers.suggested_route: No experiment; track for the day a finite-field F_2 descended-system variant appears.

papers.title: Computational Algebra with Attention: Transformer Oracles for Border Basis Algorithms
papers.authors: Hiroshi Kera, Nico Pelleriti, Yuki Ishihara, Max Zimmer, Sebastian Pokutta
papers.summary: Oracle Border Basis Algorithm: a transformer predicts which expensive reduction steps can be skipped, invoked only in critical phases, with output guarantees preserved; up to 3.5x speedup; also a sampling theorem for border bases and an O(n)-cheaper tokenisation.
papers.relevance: The 'oracle that skips reductions with correctness preserved' pattern is the honest shape for a learned F4 component: it cannot change the solving degree, only skip zero rows. The programme already has F4 trace reuse (known_mechanism row); a learned skip-predictor is its generalisation across non-identical systems.
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-2: on 10^3 descended S_4 instances at fixed (n,l), log which Macaulay rows reduce to zero at each degree; train a row-skip classifier on monomial-support features; measure fraction of zero rows predictable at >99% precision. If < 50%, the F4-trace-reuse mechanism already captures what is learnable.

papers.title: Learning selection strategies in Buchberger's algorithm
papers.authors: Dylan Peifer, Michael Stillman, Daniel Halpern-Leistner
papers.summary: PPO-trained policy for S-pair selection on random binomial ideals over Z/32003; 20-40% fewer polynomial additions than the best hand heuristics in that domain. Foundational; outside the 2024-26 window but every 2025-26 paper above builds on it.
papers.relevance: Anchor reference for the atlas item LEAD-EXO-ml-learned-models ('solver branching policy'). Nothing in the lineage has been applied over F_2 or to Weil-descent systems.
papers.suggested_route: None beyond E-ML-1/E-ML-2.

papers.title: Variables Ordering Optimization in Boolean Characteristic Set Method Using Simulated Annealing and Machine Learning-based Time Prediction
papers.authors: Minzhong Luo, Yudong Sun, Yin Long
papers.summary: For Boolean polynomial systems (algebraic cryptanalysis), trains an ML predictor of Boolean Characteristic Set (BCS) solving time from the variable frequency spectrum, then uses it as the cost in simulated annealing over variable orderings. Reports beating plain BCS, Gröbner and a SAT solver on n=m=28 training and n=32 test systems; also probabilistic complexity bounds tying predictor accuracy to expected cost.
papers.relevance: The only 2025-26 paper that does learned variable ordering for Boolean systems of cryptographic origin, which is exactly the shape of the descended S_{m+1} over F_2 (lever 1 cells). BCS/triangular-set solving is also an under-used alternative to F4/SAT in the programme (atlas LEAD-ICP-icperf-binary-pdp-solver lists WDSat/CDCL+XOR vs F4/BRiAl only).
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-3: encode descended S_4 at n=17..23, l=3..4 as Boolean systems; run a characteristic-set solver (PARI/own) under random vs frequency-spectrum-annealed orderings; compare against msolve and cryptominisat5 priced in GAE. Falsifier: BCS never within 10x of the better of msolve/SAT.

papers.title: Learning from Algorithm Feedback: One-Shot SAT Solver Guidance with GNNs (RLAF)
papers.authors: Jan Tönshoff, Martin Grohe
papers.summary: A GNN assigns per-variable weights and polarities once, injected into CDCL/look-ahead branching (Glucose, March); trained by policy gradient (GRPO) on solver runtime alone. >2x mean speedups on several distributions, generalises to larger instances, beats imitation of hand heuristics.
papers.relevance: Direct enabler for the atlas lead LEAD-ICE-sat-xor-pdp-oracle (CNF-XOR point-decomposition oracle). The pdp CNF-XOR model is a complete enumerator of V^m mod S_m, so a learned prior cannot change the exponent (generic oracle bound), but a 2x on the solve step at n=17..45 would make the unmeasured fall-degree cells cheaper to reach via SAT cross-checks.
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-4: build 5k CNF-XOR pdp instances at n=17,19 (Koblitz and random), fit a one-shot variable-weight model on cryptominisat5 conflicts; test transfer to n=23. Honest pricing: count propagations as in the lead card.

papers.title: Learning to Rank the Initial Branching Order of SAT Solvers
papers.authors: Arvid Eriksson, Gabriel Poesia, Roman Bresson, Karl Henrik Johansson, David Broman
papers.summary: GNN predicts an initial CDCL branching order; speedups on random 3-CNF and pseudo-industrial sets, generalising to larger instances, but no gain on hard industrial instances because dynamic heuristics overwrite the initial order.
papers.relevance: Negative evidence for the simplest learned-branching idea on structured hard instances; pdp CNF-XOR instances are closer to 'hard industrial' than to random 3-CNF. Supports preferring RLAF-style persistent weights over initial orders.
papers.suggested_route: Baseline arm inside E-ML-4.

papers.title: Bridging Crypto with ML-Based Solvers: The SAT Formulation and Benchmarks (SAT4CryptoBench, BASIN)
papers.authors: Xinhao Zheng, Xinhao Song, Bolin Qiu, Yang Li, Zhongteng Gui, Junchi Yan
papers.summary: First benchmark for ML-based SAT solving in cryptanalysis, in ANF and CNF, over several (unnamed in abstract) symmetric algorithms, rounds and key sizes; evaluates standalone distinguishers, learned solving heuristics and per-distribution hyperparameter tuning; proposes BASIN, a bitwise solver fed plaintext/ciphertext bitstrings. Findings: ANF networks beat CNF networks; ML struggles to generalise across algorithms and sizes; overhead can cancel gains on easy cases.
papers.relevance: ANF-native learning is the right representation for Weil-descended Semaev systems (they are ANF). The generalisation failure across sizes is the warning for any lever-1 learned component: it must be retrained per (n,l,m) cell, so it is a cost-reduction tool, not a scaling tool.
papers.suggested_route: Use SAT4CryptoBench's ANF encoding conventions when exporting pdp instances for E-ML-4 so results are comparable to the symmetric-cipher literature.

papers.title: Improving ML Attacks on LWE with Data Repetition and Stepwise Regression
papers.authors: Alberto Alfarano, Eshika Saxena, Emily Wenger, François Charton, Kristin Lauter
papers.summary: Latest Salsa-lineage result: larger training sets with repeated examples let transformers recover denser sparse secrets than before (prior ML attacks recovered <=3 cruel bits after BKZ preprocessing); empirical power law between attempts, dataset size and repetition; stepwise regression recovers cool bits; matches Cool&Cruel at n=512, log2 q=28, h=12.
papers.relevance: Defines the state of the art of 'transformer attack on a hard problem'. Key structural fact: every Salsa success is on *sparse* secrets after lattice preprocessing, i.e. the ML model exploits a planted low-weight structure, not the problem's generic hardness. ECDLP has no sparse-secret regime and no preprocessing that exposes coordinates linearly, so there is no analogue; this is a wall, not a door.
papers.suggested_route: No experiment. Record as the obstruction statement for any 'Salsa for ECDLP' proposal: name the missing ingredient (an F_p-linear leakage of the secret after a polynomial preprocessing).

papers.title: Cool + Cruel = Dual, and New Benchmarks for Sparse LWE
papers.authors: Alexander Karenin, Elena Kirshanova, Julian Nowakowski, Eamonn W. Postlethwaite, Ludo N. Pulles, Fernando Virdia, Paul Vié
papers.summary: Shows the Cool&Cruel attack that outperformed Salsa is an instance of Albrecht's 2017 dual attack and that correctly parametrised primal attacks (Drop+Solve, Guess+Verify) beat it in all regimes; open-source benchmarks.
papers.relevance: The equal-advice audit of the LWE world: an ML-adjacent 'win' reclassified as a known algorithm with a bad baseline. Exactly the programme's Bernstein-Lange audit discipline; cite when evaluating any ML cryptanalysis claim.
papers.suggested_route: Methodology only.

papers.title: TAPAS: Datasets for Learning the Learning with Errors Problem
papers.authors: Eshika Saxena, Alberto Alfarano, François Charton, Emily Wenger, Kristin Lauter
papers.summary: Public LWE datasets with SALSA and Cool&Cruel baselines so ML practitioners can prototype attacks without lattice preprocessing infrastructure.
papers.relevance: Model for what a public 'ECDLP index-calculus dataset' would look like (descended systems + certified degrees + priced costs); the sibling repo's data/*.jsonl already plays this role internally but is not published.
papers.suggested_route: Programme hygiene: consider exporting the n=13-45 fall-degree table in a TAPAS-like format so external ML groups can try lever 1 cells.

papers.title: NoMod: A Non-modular Attack on Module Learning With Errors
papers.authors: Cristian Bassotto, Ermes Franch, Marina Krček, Stjepan Picek
papers.summary: Hybrid attack treating modular wrap-around as noise and recovering secrets by robust linear estimation (Tukey biweight loss) after lattice preprocessing; recovers binary secrets at n=350, sparse binomial at n=256, Kyber-like sparse settings.
papers.relevance: Again linear-after-preprocessing sparse-secret regime. No ECDLP analogue; included to complete the 2025 picture of the ML-LWE lineage.
papers.suggested_route: None.

papers.title: Discovering Lattice Reduction Strategies via Self-Play (DeltaStar)
papers.authors: Mohamed Malhou, Kristin Lauter, Ludovic Perret
papers.summary: Lattice reduction as a single-player MDP; AlphaZero-style self-play with adaptive-horizon MCTS over primitive row operations; trained on 8-dim q-ary lattices, uses fewer primitive operations than LLL and transfers to unseen moduli and dimensions up to 32. No BKZ comparison.
papers.relevance: Only lever-3-adjacent ML result found (small-root method for S_5 at delta~1/5 needs a better lattice step, not a faster LLL). Learned reduction cannot raise the Jochemsz-May reach delta_max, which is a shape bound on the lattice, so this is engineering for the never-run D_4-symmetrised S_5 lattice at best.
papers.suggested_route: None for ML; the D_4-symmetrised S_5 run itself (lever 3) should be done with fplll first.

papers.title: Anthropic: key-recovery attack on HAWK-256 found by Claude Mythos Preview (HAWK withdrawn from NIST additional-signatures process)
papers.authors: Anthropic (model-assisted); HAWK team withdrawal notice
papers.summary: Per hawk-sign.info (verified): HAWK withdrawn 29 July 2026 'because Anthropic discovered a new attack that approximately halves the block size required in lattice reduction' to recover an equivalent private key. Per secondary press (unverified): the model identified a previously unused symmetry (automorphism) of HAWK's lattice, built a tau-cocycle lattice from the public key, and reduced the HAWK-256 work factor from ~2^64 to ~2^38 (3h42m on 96 cores); attack remains exponential and does not extend to ML-DSA/ML-KEM. Same release reportedly includes a 200-800x refinement of a 7-round AES-128 MITM attack (still 2^105 data).
papers.relevance: The strongest 2025-26 'AI mathematician on lattices' datum and the only one with a confirmed real-world consequence. Mechanism is instructive for this programme: an *unused symmetry of the public structure* halved a block size, i.e. a constant-factor-in-exponent gain inside a known algorithm; it did not change the algorithm's exponent class. This matches the programme's Symmetry-inventory closure (symmetry cannot change an exponent but can make decisive cells affordable). For ECDLP the inventory is already enumerated (negation, Frobenius, CM, 2-torsion, S_m, D_4 on S_5) and D_4 on S_5 is the one computed-but-never-run item.
papers.suggested_route: Not an experiment on HAWK. Programme action: run the D_4-symmetrised S_5 lattice (lever 3) — it is the exact analogue of 'an enumerated but unexploited symmetry' — and have an agent-driven search re-audit the symmetry inventory of the descended S_4/S_5 systems for any automorphism of the *presentation* (e.g. ONB-II permutation structure of F_{2^131}, mu_263 action) not yet in the table.

papers.title: CryptanalysisBench: Can LLMs do Cryptanalysis?
papers.authors: Lukas Fluri, Avital Shafran, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Milad Nasr, Orr Dunkelman, Eyal Ronen, Florian Tramèr
papers.summary: 191 tasks over six primitive families (mostly NIST competition submissions) in three tiers with game-based verification; frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8/Sonnet 5/Mythos 5, GPT 5.5, GLM 5.2) break 65-86% of tier-1 (known-break) schemes, 6-12 full-strength tier-2 schemes, and produce two novel results (SpoC key recovery, KINDI proof error) under 2h budgets.
papers.relevance: Calibrates what agent swarms (like this one) can and cannot do: wins are on design flaws of symmetric/KEM candidates, none on ECDLP/number-theoretic hardness. No elliptic-curve or DLP tasks in the benchmark.
papers.suggested_route: Methodology: adopt their verification-game framing for the programme's falsifier experiments (every claim has an automatic checker).

papers.title: AI Grinding for Fun and Cryptanalysis
papers.authors: Lukasz Olejnik, Bartosz Naskrecki
papers.summary: Agent-driven hypothesis generate/test/refine workflow with human adjudication; reports eight published constructions failing at stated parameters (Ring-LWR commitment, middle-product encryption leak, lattice e-voting receipt-freeness, updatable encryption, an explicit normal basis splitting a degree-63 instance into seven degree-9 instances, a hash collision, a noise-threshold oracle) plus two assumption-level failures (group-ring decision, MinRank hardening). Each with an exact witness and control.
papers.relevance: The 'normal basis splits degree-63 into 7x degree-9' item is the one number-theoretic flavour: a presentation/subfield-structure exploit, which is exactly the door the programme has closed at prime n=131 (no proper subfield, ord_131(2)=130). Confirms agent workflows find *presentation* leaks, which is where lever 6 (non-subspace Frobenius-stable bases) lives.
papers.suggested_route: Feed lever 6 (trace-spectrum, Hamming-ball, mu_263 bases at n=131) to an agent-grinding loop with the exact-witness-plus-control discipline; the brief's A2 cyclotomic-sparse base is never measured.

papers.title: ECDSA.Fail: Open Autoresearch for Optimizing Elliptic-Curve Point Addition in Shor's Algorithm
papers.authors: Jieyi Long, Theodore Pender, Zhao Huang, et al. (35 authors)
papers.summary: Humans and AI agents submit evaluator-verified improvements to a public leaderboard for reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits (score Q x T); 86.1% reduction; best 1,151 qubits / 1.30M Toffoli at cutoff (Q x T ~1.5e9), later 1.26e9; windowed-compatible variant at ~0.998 success.
papers.relevance: Quantum-circuit engineering, not classical ECDLP; included because it is the one 2026 agent-driven ECDLP-adjacent programme and the environment already carries an ecdsafail-cli skill, so it is presumably known. Shows the autoresearch loop works when there is a verifiable scalar score; the classical IC programme has that (GAE S = ops/sqrt(r)) and could expose the fall-degree grid the same way.
papers.suggested_route: Programme hygiene: publish the (n,l,m) fall-degree cells and the price-band GAE as an open leaderboard.

papers.title: Mage: Cracking Elliptic Curve Cryptography with Cross-Axis Transformers
papers.authors: Lily Erickson
papers.summary: Asks whether language-model architectures can learn the public->private key map on secp256r1 or memorise keypairs; abstract states aims only, reports no success and no quantified negative result.
papers.relevance: The only paper found that literally tries 'transformer vs ECDLP'; it is result-free. Theoretical reason it must fail at scale is Takhanov et al. (below). Record so it is not re-proposed.
papers.suggested_route: None.

papers.title: Intractability of Learning the Discrete Logarithm with Gradient-Based Methods
papers.authors: Rustem Takhanov, Maxat Tezekbayev, Artur Pak, Arman Bolatov, Zhibek Kadyrsizova, Zhenisbek Assylbekov
papers.summary: Proves the gradient of the loss for learning the parity bit of a discrete logarithm in a prime-order cyclic group concentrates around a base-independent fixed point, so gradient-based learning is restricted regardless of architecture; experiments agree.
papers.relevance: The theorem-level obstruction for 'neural ECDLP' (atlas LEAD-EXO-ml-learned-models' first item, 'learn a predictor of log bits'). Outside the date window but it is the kill statement every 2025-26 grokking paper has to reckon with. Scope: applies to end-to-end learning of log bits from group elements; does not bound learned heuristics inside an algebraic solver.
papers.suggested_route: Cite as the obstruction in the ML lead card; close the 'learn log bits' sub-item of LEAD-EXO-ml-learned-models as closed_obstructed.

papers.title: The Discrete-Log Clock: How a Transformer Learns Modular Multiplication
papers.authors: Huu Danh Nguyen
papers.summary: Reverse-engineers a grokked 1-layer transformer on a*b mod 113: in the multiplicative-character basis the embedding is sparse (~4 frequencies), i.e. the model maps multiplication to addition in discrete-log space. Analysis limited to p=113.
papers.relevance: Mechanistically the network *uses* a discrete-log table it memorised for p=113; it does not compute logs. Confirms that grokking results on tiny p are table lookups in disguise, consistent with Takhanov et al.
papers.suggested_route: None.

papers.title: Grokking the Discrete Logarithm: Scaling Across Model Capacity and Mechanistic Analysis
papers.authors: not verified (Research Square preprint; companion repo VesterlundCoder/dlp-grokking)
papers.summary: UNVERIFIED (page returned title only; details from search snippets): 427k-parameter 2-layer transformer reaches 99.8% test accuracy on variable-base DLP at p=113 after long memorisation; capacity sweep 90k-14.4M params shows grokking at the anchor and again 1.64M-14.4M; transition aligns with multiplicative-character structure; symbolic regression on hidden states recovers character-aligned trig features; prime-order and disjoint-generator controls.
papers.relevance: Within the 'past few weeks' window. Still p=113 memorisation; no scaling claim toward cryptographic sizes; the 'symbolic regression recovers character features' is the same lesson as the Discrete-Log Clock.
papers.suggested_route: None; monitor for any p>2^20 result (would contradict Takhanov et al. and be worth a replication).

papers.title: Murmurations: a case study in AI-assisted mathematics
papers.authors: Yang-Hui He, Kyu-Hwan Lee, Thomas Oliver, Alexey Pozdnyakov
papers.summary: Retrospective on the murmuration phenomenon (oscillating averages of a_p over isogeny classes ordered by conductor), found via ML interpretability and then proved for several families (Sawin-Sutherland 2025 explicit density for height ordering); places it in the context of BSD and random matrix theory.
papers.relevance: The canonical success of 'ML finds a number-theoretic law' is an *averaged* statistic over families, invisible on a single curve. For ECDLP the analogue would be a law over the factor-base locus of one fixed curve; the programme's bias hunts (coordinate statistics) are exhausted_at_scale and character-sum pseudorandomness is closed. So murmuration-style discovery has no obvious target here unless the quantity is the yield *variance* (left free by the monodromy closure).
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-5 (cheap): over the n=17..23 ladders, compute per-target decomposition counts and test whether their variance (not mean) across targets carries any family-level signal in trace/Frobenius-orbit features with the sibling repo's permutation null. Mean is a double count (closed); variance is open.

papers.title: Decision trees, Frobenius traces, and Weierstrass coefficients of elliptic curves
papers.authors: Barinder S. Banwait, Xiaoyu Huang, Kyu-Hwan Lee, Seewoo Lee, Thomas Oliver, Alexey Pozdnyakov
papers.summary: Decision trees on LMFDB data suggested, and the authors then proved, explicit formulas for three reduced-minimal-Weierstrass coefficients in terms of a_2, a_3, a_4, and congruences for two more mod 5 and mod 7 from a_5, a_7.
papers.relevance: Best 2026 example of the exact-rule-mining pattern the sibling repo uses (csd/mine.py: constant/equality/offset rules, zero-violation check). The discovered laws are local (reduction mod small primes), which is the kind of law that *could* exist for the descended system: e.g. congruence constraints between coordinates of decomposable targets. The programme's bit-level/coordinate bias hunts are exhausted at scale, but exact-rule mining with zero-violation certificates was only run on isogeny-graph observables (M2), not on decomposability.
papers.suggested_route: Experiment E-ML-6: run csd/mine.py's exact-rule miner on (target, decomposable?) tables at n=13..19 with the lab's residue/character/bit-plane vocabulary; require zero violations on a complete enumeration and a fresh n. Expected answer per the closures: null. A non-null exact rule would be a non-group filter (KN-OPEN-91d4f6).

papers.title: Transformers Learn the Mestre-Nagao Heuristic
papers.authors: Pranav Venkata Konda
papers.summary: 2-layer transformer on 128 normalised a_p classifies rank 0 vs 1 for conductor <= 10^4 at >99%; ~20 first-layer neurons suffice and the top neuron's input weights match Mestre-Nagao weights; CLS attention on prime positions encodes log L(E,1).
papers.relevance: Shows interpretability can read a known analytic-number-theory functional off a trained model. If any learned decomposability or hardness model in the sibling repo ever beats null, the same probe would say which functional it found; until then, no action.
papers.suggested_route: Methodology only.

papers.relevance: Leakage lesson. The sibling repo already groups splits by (p,|t|) so twists never cross a split (PLAN.md), so the control is in place; cite it as external confirmation of that design choice.

lever_1_fall_degree_cells.what_a_learned_component_can_realistical: Nothing to the exponent: d_F is a property of the ideal plus presentation and is measured by a certificate, not predicted. A learned component can (a) pick the presentation (F_2-basis of V, variable/monomial order) that minimises msolve time for a fixed cell (Bunch et al. 2602.02972 template; Luo et al. 2509.14754 for Boolean systems), (b) predict zero-reducing Macaulay rows to skip (Kera et al. 2505.23696 pattern, generalising F4 trace reuse), (c) supply one-shot SAT variable weights for CNF-XOR cross-checks (RLAF 2505.16053). Realistic combined gain 2-10x in wall time on cells (4,4),(4,5),(4,6), which is the difference between 'unmeasured' and 'measured'. Classification: engineering/enabler.
lever_1_fall_degree_cells.falsifiers: E-ML-1: if msolve time variance over presentations at fixed cell is < 2x, drop (a). E-ML-2: if < 50% of zero rows are predictable at 99% precision, drop (b). E-ML-4: if learned SAT priors give < 1.5x on n=19 after training on n=17, drop (c).
lever_1_fall_degree_cells.what_it_cannot_do: Change d_F or D; the Generic-oracle and GGM closures apply unchanged because none of these components reads the field representation differently from the solver they accelerate.

lever_12_ml_predictors.what_the_sweep_adds: No external result in 2024-26 learns anything about decomposability or solving degree of Weil-descent systems; the sibling repo is ahead of the public literature. Two external methods are worth importing: exact-rule mining with zero-violation certificates applied to decomposability tables (Banwait et al. 2607.24251 shows the pattern yields provable congruence laws), and yield-variance (not mean) as the target, since mean yield is closed by the monodromy lemma and variance is explicitly left free.
lever_12_ml_predictors.falsifiers: E-ML-6 (exact rules on decomposability at n=13..19, complete enumeration, fresh n) and E-ML-5 (variance of per-target decomposition counts vs permutation null). Pre-registered expectation: null for both; a non-null is a candidate x-functional filter (KN-OPEN-91d4f6).
lever_12_ml_predictors.obstruction_to_record: Takhanov et al. 2310.01611: gradient learning of log bits is blocked independent of architecture; close the 'learn a predictor of log bits' sub-item of LEAD-EXO-ml-learned-models.

proposals_for_levers.cross_lever_note: The one 2026 event where an AI system changed a security estimate (HAWK, July 2026) worked by exploiting an enumerated-but-unused symmetry inside a known algorithm (lattice reduction block size halved). The programme's analogue is the D_4-symmetrised S_5 lattice (lever 3), computed on paper and never run. That is the cheapest 'AI mathematician'-style action available here and needs no ML.
